overview:
Caturvimshatistava (often found under the title *Chaturviṃśatitīrthaṅkara Stuti* or *Homage to the Twenty‑four Tirthankaras*) is a Sanskrit hymn devoted to praising all twenty‑four Tirthankaras of the current avasarpinī (descending time‑cycle) in Jain cosmology. The term *catur‑vimśati* means “twenty‑four,” and *stava* or *stuti* means “hymn of praise.” As a devotional composition, it belongs to the broad Jain tradition of collective eulogies (stava, stuti, vandanā) that focus on the qualities of the Jinas rather than petitionary prayer.

The hymn systematically celebrates the spiritual accomplishments and distinctive attributes of each Tirthankara, beginning with Ṛṣabhanātha (Ādinātha) and ending with Vardhamāna Mahāvīra. In its opening verse, the text bows to the Tirthankaras as beings who bear the thousand‑and‑eight auspicious marks, have crossed the ocean of knowledge, destroyed the web of saṃsāra, and shine with radiance surpassing the sun and moon. Subsequent verses mention each Tirthankara by name, often with brief epithets that recall narrative traditions—such as lineage, special virtues (like kṣamā, forgiveness, or brahmacarya, celibacy), and their role as teachers of dharma.

Caturvimshatistava is used in both temple and home settings as a recited hymn, especially in contexts where the entire lineage of twenty‑four Tirthankaras is being remembered. Its language is classical Sanskrit, but it is transmitted in multiple scripts and transliteration schemes (Devanāgarī, Roman, Gujarati, Tamil, etc.), reflecting its pan‑Jain devotional use. The text is not a canonical āgama but a later liturgical composition that draws on canonical and narrative materials to construct a concise, poetic homage. Because it focuses on praise rather than doctrinal exposition, it is often recommended for lay practitioners and youth as an accessible way to internalize the names and basic qualities of the Tirthankaras.

From a doctrinal perspective, the hymn reinforces central Jain themes: the omniscience (sarvajñatā) of the Jinas, their complete destruction of karmic bondage, their status as teachers of true dharma, and their role as exemplars for aspirants on the path of liberation. The verses also highlight the reverence offered to the Tirthankaras by celestial beings, ascetics, and lay followers, situating Jain devotion within a cosmological framework. In contemporary practice, Caturvimshatistava is sometimes combined with other stotras (such as individual Tirthankara hymns) in daily pūjā or svādhyāya, and it is cited in community education materials as a compact summary of the twenty‑four Tirthankaras’ names and virtues.

Scholarly and community editions classify the text within the category of Jain devotional literature (stava‑saṅgraha), often accompanied by translations and explanatory notes. While there may be minor variations in wording or orthography across manuscripts and printed editions, the core sequence of verses and the list of twenty‑four Tirthankaras remain stable. As with many liturgical texts, interpretation of Caturvimshatistava benefits from reading it alongside narrative sources (like *Kalpa‑sūtra* and later Jain caritras) and doctrinal works that explain the qualities being praised, such as omniscience, non‑violence, and the destruction of karma.

primary_sources.title: Chaturviṃśatitīrthaṅkara Stuti (Caturvimshatistava)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally anonymous; transmitted in Jain devotional collections
primary_sources.original_text:
ये लोकेऽष्टसहस्रलक्षणधरा ज्ञेयार्णवान्तं गता  
ये सम्यग्भवजालहेतुमथनाश्चन्द्रार्कतेजोऽधिकाः ।  
ये साध्विन्द्रसुराप्सरोगणशतैर्गीतप्रणत्यार्चिता-  
स्तान् देवान्वृषभादिवीरचरमान् भक्त्या नमस्याम्यहम् ॥ १॥

नाभेयं देवपूज्यं जिनवरमजितं सर्वलोकप्रदीपं  
सर्वज्ञं सम्भवाख्यं मुनिगणवृषभं नन्दनं देवदेवम् ।  
कर्मारिघ्नं सुबुद्धिं वरकमलनिभं पद्मपुष्पाभिगन्धं  
क्षान्तं दान्तं सुपार्श्वं सकलशशिनिभं चन्द्रमानानमीडे ॥ २॥

ye loke.aṣṭasahasralakṣaṇadharā jñeyārṇavāntaṃ gatā

ye sādhvindrasurāpsarogaṇaśatairgītapraṇatyārcitā-  
stān devān vṛṣabhādivīracaramān bhaktyā namasyāmyaham || 1||

nābheyaṃ devapūjyaṃ jinavaramajitaṃ sarvalokapradīpaṃ

karmārighnaṃ subuddhiṃ varakamalanibhaṃ padmapuṣpābhigandhaṃ  
kṣāntaṃ dāntaṃ supārśvaṃ sakalaśaśinibhaṃ candramānānamīḍe || 2||
primary_sources.translation:
1. I shall bow with devotion to those radiant ones, the Tirthankaras, from Ṛṣabhanātha to Mahāvīra. In this world, they bore the thousand‑and‑eight auspicious signs; they crossed the ocean of knowledge; truly destroyed the web of transmigration; were more radiant than the moon and the sun; and were worshipped through musical hymns by multitudes of monks, celestial divinities, their lords, and celestial nymphs.

2. Nabheya (the son of King Nābhirāja), Ṛṣabhanātha, is worshipped by celestial beings. Ajitanātha enlightens the whole world. Saṃbhavanātha is omniscient. Best among ascetics, Abhinandananātha is worshipped by demi‑gods. Sumatinātha is the destroyer of the enemy named karma. Padmaprabha has lotus‑like fragrance and complexion. Suparśvanātha is full of forgiveness and has conquered his senses. Candraprabha has the splendour of the full moon. I worship all the Jinas with absolute reverence.
primary_sources.notes: Corpus tier: A/B (primary liturgical text with reviewed transliteration and translation). The verses cited here are taken from a widely circulated Sanskrit devotional edition of *chaturviṃśatitīrthaṅkara stutiḥ*, prepared and proofread by Jain scholars and volunteers for personal study and research. The first verse functions as a general homage to all twenty‑four Tirthankaras, emphasizing their auspicious marks, omniscience, and destruction of saṃsāra. The second verse begins the sequential praise of individual Tirthankaras, starting with Ṛṣabhanātha and continuing through Ajitanātha, Saṃbhavanātha, Abhinandananātha, Sumatinātha, Padmaprabha, Suparśvanātha, and Candraprabha. Different editions may vary slightly in punctuation, sandhi resolution, or orthography, but the core wording and sequence are consistent. For a fuller study, the remaining verses should be consulted in a complete, verified edition, and read alongside narrative sources that explain the epithets and biographical references.

misconceptions.myth: Caturvimshatistava is a canonical Jain āgama with binding doctrinal authority equal to the scriptures.
misconceptions.reality: Caturvimshatistava is a later devotional hymn (stava/stuti), not part of the canonical āgamas. It is respected and widely used in liturgical practice, but doctrinal and disciplinary questions are grounded in the canonical texts and in the guidance of qualified teachers from living lineages.

misconceptions.myth: Reciting Caturvimshatistava by itself guarantees liberation, regardless of one’s conduct or understanding.
misconceptions.reality: Jain tradition presents hymns like Caturvimshatistava as supports for devotion, recollection of the Jinas, and inspiration toward right faith, knowledge, and conduct. Liberation (mokṣa) requires the complete destruction of karmas through sustained ethical discipline, meditation, and right view; mere recitation without corresponding transformation of conduct is not considered sufficient.

misconceptions.myth: The hymn gives detailed philosophical teachings, so it can replace study of doctrinal texts such as the Tattvārtha‑sūtra.
misconceptions.reality: Caturvimshatistava is primarily poetic praise and brief characterization of the Tirthankaras. It alludes to doctrinal themes (omniscience, destruction of karma, true dharma) but does not systematically expound them. For technical understanding of Jain philosophy—such as tattvas, guṇasthānas, and karma theory—foundational doctrinal works and qualified teachers are necessary.

misconceptions.myth: Only one Jain sect uses Caturvimshatistava; it is exclusive to a particular tradition.
misconceptions.reality: Because the hymn simply praises the twenty‑four Tirthankaras recognized across Jain traditions, it appears in multiple sectarian contexts and script traditions. While specific liturgical settings and commentarial interpretations may differ between Digambara and Śvetāmbara communities, the basic text and its devotional function are shared.
